title: Volumes and Bind Mounts
intro: Containers are ephemeral — anything written inside one disappears when it's removed, unless you deliberately persist it with a volume or bind mount.

steps.explanation: This creates storage managed by Docker itself, independent of any container's lifecycle.
steps.why: You could skip this and let 'docker run -v db-data:/path' auto-create it on first use — creating it explicitly first is mainly useful when you want to configure it (a driver, labels) before anything attaches to it.

steps.prompt: Run a postgres container using that named volume for /var/lib/postgresql/data.
steps.explanation: Now the database files live in the 'db-data' volume, not inside the container's own writable layer.
steps.why: A bind mount (-v /host/absolute/path:/container/path) would work too, but a named volume is the better default for data you want Docker to manage — it isn't tied to a specific host path, so it works the same way across different machines.

steps.prompt: List all volumes to confirm it's there.
steps.explanation: This just lists volume names — it won't tell you which containers are actually using each one.
steps.why: For that, you'd need 'docker volume inspect db-data' or cross-reference with 'docker inspect' on the container — 'volume ls' is just the quick existence check.

steps.prompt: Remove the container, then bind-mount your current directory's ./config folder to /etc/app/config in a new one (read-only).
steps.explanation: :ro makes the mount read-only inside the container — the app can read config files but can't accidentally modify your host files.
steps.why: A bind mount (a host path, not a named volume) is what you want here specifically because you need to edit config files on your host and have the container see the change immediately — a named volume's contents aren't meant to be edited from outside Docker like that.

steps.prompt: You're done experimenting — remove the unused 'db-data' volume.
steps.explanation: This permanently deletes the volume's data — only works if no running container is currently using it.
steps.why: Docker refuses to remove a volume that's still attached to a container, even a stopped one, specifically to prevent accidentally destroying data that something still references — you'd need to remove the container first if this failed.
